prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. After the first round the case rests on three points that survived the objections. First, the magic-wavelength condition is a distinct physical idea: it makes it possible to interrogate very many neutral atoms, tightly confined, without the trap shifting the clock transition. The comb of 2005 supplied the means of counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems; neither addresses the statistical limit that the lattice removes. Second, the result is mature in the sense that matters: independent laboratories compare lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level, and the systematic budgets (polarisabilities, blackbody shifts, higher-order light shifts, collisional and many-body effects) are atomic-structure problems of real depth, which I can assess directly as an atomic theorist. Third, the credit is compact. Katori proposed the scheme and made the first demonstrations, and Ye's group took the accuracy and stability frontier and the many-body clock physics further. The consequences are already measurable in tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and they do not depend on when the second is redefined.
statement.case_against: The lineage objection from Danielsson, Kroll, Pearce and Olsson remains the serious one, and I cannot show that it is wrong; I can only say that I find the answer above persuasive, and a colleague who weighs the 2005 and 2012 prizes more heavily could reasonably wait. The second objection is credit at the edges: Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow, Gill and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names, and ion clocks reach comparable accuracy. A two-name prize therefore rests on a citation that must be worded to the lattice scheme specifically, not to optical clocks in general. Third, I rank this first from within my own subfield, and I should discount my confidence for that. Finally, my weakest evidence is on priority at the margin: several strontium demonstrations appeared at about the same time, and the supplied record does not let me settle who did what within weeks.

responses.point: Kroll prefers honouring the lattice scheme specifically, leaving ion clocks as a parallel route for a later year, and would stay open to wording that does not exclude them in principle.
responses.response: I agree, and I now think that is the correct line to hold. Adding an ion-clock name would dilute the one concept that makes this a distinct achievement, and none of those names is on the shortlist in any case. I would put into the citation both the invention of the scheme and the development to 10^-18, so that Ye's accuracy and many-body contribution is stated explicitly and not left implied. I also accept your point that the pending redefinition of the second is no reason to act now, and I would not use it as an argument either way; I disagree with treating it as timeliness.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks circuit QED first and lattice clocks only fifth, and in his round-1 text names the credit boundary around Girvin and Huang as the main weakness of a Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf trio.
responses.response: I take your chair question seriously: if only one of B016 and B031 could proceed, I would choose B031, and the evidence that would change that is a settled position on Girvin and Huang. Circuit QED is a mature and important architecture and I would be content to see it recognised, but a trio drawn from a founding proposal with five authors and an experiment with a larger Yale team leaves unresolved credit in a way the lattice pair does not. I also note that you describe the circuit QED citation as needing to separate it from the 2025 prize. I think that can be done, but it requires careful wording, while the clock case needs no such repair beyond the lineage point.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that circuit QED is a single sharply defined idea with a clean theory-plus-experiment split, and that the citation should be kept narrow, to strong coupling and dispersive readout, so that the trio holds.
responses.response: That narrow wording does make the trio more defensible, and I accept it as a real improvement over a citation naming quantum computing hardware. I also agree that the 2025 prize and this one are different discoveries, as I said in round 1. My remaining difficulty is that a narrow citation separates the architecture from the transmon and the Yale readout work that gave it its practical standing, so the prize would honour the idea without the achievements that made it consequential. For the clock, the idea and the demonstration are in the same two names. That asymmetry is why I put B031 first, although I respect that you weigh it the other way and I would not call circuit QED an unsafe choice.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the experimental Higgs discovery and weighs the clock work fifth because of the 2005 prize and the unsettled timing of the redefinition.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs is the most obvious discovery in the strict sense, and that the experimental half has gone unrecognised. My difficulty, which you concede yourself, is that no three names from Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti can be defended against the others, and a prize whose credit is that open to challenge is weaker, in my judgement, than one that is a discovery in a looser sense but cleanly attributed. On the 2005 prize I stand by my answer: the comb is the tool for counting the cycles, while the lattice solves a separate problem. I would not move the redefinition to the centre of the argument, and I do not think it is a reason to delay.

responses.point: Olsson regards the magic-wavelength condition as a distinct invention and the 10^-18 systematic budget as a different kind of result from the comb, and says the case should state explicitly what is new.
responses.response: I agree and have tried to follow your advice: the new element is a trapping condition under which the trap does not shift the clock frequency, together with a demonstration that the many-atom systematics can be controlled to 10^-18. I would keep that in the citation. I also appreciate that you moved your own first choice out of the way because of proximity, and I would hold my own ranking to the same standard. I weigh my subfield judgement as one input among several, and I would not wish the committee to take my first place as more than it is.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize; this is the point on which colleagues' judgement could reasonably differ from mine.

Whether the two-name credit can withstand the objection that Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow, Gill and the ion-clock groups made real contributions; I cannot settle priority within the supplied record.
How circuit QED compares with clocks once the Girvin and Huang question is settled; I have kept B016 as my first alternative because I regard it as mature and important.
Whether a prize in this area is better given now or after the redefinition of the second, on which I do not think the discovery depends but which others weigh differently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B031: my profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I do collaborate with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and Andreas Wallraff (credited under B016, my first alternative) is at the same institution; I disclosed this as a possible recusal question if B016 advances, and I maintain that disclosure. I know of no direct tie to him. My own first place for B031 reflects my subfield, and I mention that so colleagues can weigh it accordingly.
